\chapter{More Than One}
\label{ch:ur-more-than-one}
\hlchaptermodality{25}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can make a noun plural, and I can make it plural before a postposition, which is the one ending in Urdu that is never ambiguous.}

No noun in this book had ever been more than one. The four-cell table closes, two of its cells collide on purpose, and \ur{ہم} gives the track its first plural pronoun and its first plural possessive.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kamre]{\ur{کمرے} (kamre) — more than one}

\label{lesson:UR-C25-plural}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{in the room}, and say what the noun had to do first.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the postposition that marks the one a thing is done to — \emph{ko}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the plural}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} — \emph{kamrā} — a room.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کمرے}} — \emph{kamre} — \textbf{rooms.}
\end{quote}

Twenty-four chapters, and no noun in this book has ever been more than one.

Look hard at the plural, because you have seen it before. \textbf{\ur{کمرے}} is exactly the oblique singular from chapter twenty-three — same three letters, same sound. Urdu spells \emph{rooms} and \emph{of the room} identically and lets the rest of the sentence tell them apart.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the table, and what the postposition settles}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{one} & \textbf{more than one} \\
\midrule
direct & \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} & \textbf{\ur{کمرے}} \\
oblique & \textbf{\ur{کمرے}} & \emph{next lesson} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of the four cells are filled and two of them look the same. A postposition settles it: \textbf{\ur{کمرے} \ur{میں}} can only be \emph{in the room}, because a plural before a postposition takes a different shape again — which is the next lesson.

Nouns not ending in \emph{-ā} do not change at all. \textbf{\ur{ماں}} is one mother or several and is spelled \textbf{\ur{ماں}} either way, so number, like the oblique, is often invisible in Urdu and has to be read off the sentence.

And the adjective agrees: \textbf{\ur{کالا} \ur{کمرہ}} $\to$ \textbf{\ur{کالے} \ur{کمرے}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kamrā}, then \emph{kamre}
  \item the two readings of one spelling — \emph{kamre} (rooms), \emph{kamre meṅ} (in the room)
  \item with the adjective agreeing — \emph{kāle kamre}
  \item the one that does not move — \emph{māṅ}, one or many
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the plural of \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}}? (\textbf{\ur{کمرے}}.) What else is spelled that way? (\textbf{The oblique singular}.) What tells them apart? (\textbf{Whether a postposition follows}.) And which nouns show no plural at all? (\textbf{Those not ending in -\ur{ا}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kamroṅ]{\ur{کمروں} (kamroṅ) — more than one, before a postposition}

\label{lesson:UR-C25-oblique-plural}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{rooms}. Then say \textbf{in the room}, and say why those two are spelled the same.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{کمروں}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کمروں} \ur{میں}} — \emph{kamroṅ meṅ} — \textbf{in the rooms.}
\end{quote}

Here is the fourth cell, and it is the one that removes the ambiguity:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{one} & \textbf{more than one} \\
\midrule
direct & \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} & \textbf{\ur{کمرے}} \\
oblique & \textbf{\ur{کمرے}} & \textbf{\ur{کمروں}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{-\ur{وں}} is unmistakable. Nothing else in Urdu ends that way, so a reader who meets it knows immediately that the noun is plural \textbf{and} that a postposition is coming.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending that catches every noun}]
This is the one place where \textbf{every} Urdu noun changes visibly, including the ones that have refused to move so far. \textbf{\ur{کان}} is one ear or two and is spelled the same either way, and it does not mark an oblique — but put it in the plural \textbf{and} in front of a postposition and it becomes \textbf{\ur{کانوں}}.

So the rule to hold is: \textbf{-\ur{وں}} on the end means \emph{plural, and something is coming after me.}

That final \textbf{\ur{ں}} is the nūn-e-ghunna of chapter one — the nasal with no dots that colours the vowel rather than sounding as an \emph{n}. The same letter ends \textbf{\ur{ہاں}} and \textbf{\ur{کہاں}} and \textbf{\ur{یہاں}}.

And the demonstrative in front of it is already yours: the plural oblique \textbf{\ur{ان}} from the last chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kamroṅ meṅ}
  \item all four cells — \emph{kamrā}, \emph{kamre}, \emph{kamre meṅ}, \emph{kamroṅ meṅ}
  \item with the demonstrative — \emph{un kamroṅ meṅ}
  \item the noun that finally moves — \emph{kān}, then \emph{kānoṅ ko}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{-\ur{وں}} tell you, in two parts? (\textbf{Plural}, and \textbf{a postposition is coming}.) Is it ever ambiguous? (\textbf{No} — nothing else ends that way.) And which letter is at the end of it? (\textbf{The nūn-e-ghunna}, the dotless nasal.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ham]{\ur{ہم} (ham) — we}

\label{lesson:UR-C25-hum}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{I}. Then name the three words for \textbf{you}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{ہم}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ہم} \ur{یہاں} \ur{ہیں}} — \emph{ham yahāṅ haiṅ} — \textbf{we are here.}
\end{quote}

Twenty-four chapters of this book have been about one person at a time. \textbf{\ur{میں}} or \textbf{\ur{آپ}}, and nobody else. \textbf{\ur{ہم}} is the first pronoun that covers a group.

Notice the verb. \textbf{\ur{میں} … \ur{ہوں}} but \textbf{\ur{ہم} … \ur{ہیں}}: the plural subject takes the plural form of \emph{to be}, and it is the same \textbf{\ur{ہیں}} you have been saying to \textbf{\ur{آپ}} since chapter four.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{} that is sometimes one person}]
Urdu does the same thing with \textbf{\ur{ہم}} that it does with \textbf{\ur{آپ}} and \textbf{\ur{ان}}: a plural form used of one person, for distance and formality.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{grammatically} & \textbf{often used for} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ur{آپ}} & you, plural & one person, respectfully \\
\textbf{\ur{ان}} & those & one person, respectfully \\
\textbf{\ur{ہم}} & we & one speaker, formally \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A speaker who says \textbf{\ur{ہم}} of themselves is being formal or a little grand, and in much of Pakistan it is the ordinary way to say \emph{I} in some registers. A learner should say \textbf{\ur{میں}} and should recognise \textbf{\ur{ہم}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ham yahāṅ haiṅ}
  \item the singular and the plural — \emph{maiṅ yahāṅ hūṅ}, \emph{ham yahāṅ haiṅ}
  \item \emph{ham kamre meṅ haiṅ}
  \item the three plural-for-one forms — \emph{āp}, \emph{un}, \emph{ham}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form of \emph{to be} follows \textbf{\ur{ہم}}? (\textbf{\ur{ہیں}}.) What else can \textbf{\ur{ہم}} mean besides \emph{we}? (\textbf{A formal \emph{I}}.) And which two other words in this book use a plural for one person? (\textbf{\ur{آپ}} and \textbf{\ur{ان}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hamārā]{\ur{ہمارا} (hamārā) — our}

\label{lesson:UR-C25-hamara}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{we}. Then say \textbf{my name} and \textbf{your name}, and notice that one of them has a separate little word in it and the other does not.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{ہمارا}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ہمارا} \ur{کمرہ}} — \emph{hamārā kamrā} — \textbf{our room.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ہماری} \ur{ماں}} — \emph{hamārī māṅ} — \textbf{our mother.}
\end{quote}

And now the thing worth seeing. \textbf{\ur{میرا}} has looked like a word since chapter two and it is not one:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ur{آپ} \ur{کا}} — \emph{āp kā} — pronoun, then \textbf{\ur{کا}}, written apart
  \item \textbf{\ur{میرا}} — \emph{merā} — pronoun and \textbf{\ur{کا}}, fused
  \item \textbf{\ur{ہمارا}} — \emph{hamārā} — pronoun and \textbf{\ur{کا}}, fused
\end{itemize}

All three are the same construction. The first person fuses and the respectful second person does not, which is an accident of wear, not a difference of grammar.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the possessive agrees, like any adjective}]
\textbf{\ur{کا}} ends in \textbf{-\ur{ا}}, so it behaves like \textbf{\ur{کالا}} and \textbf{\ur{پرانا}} and changes with the noun after it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the noun is} & \textbf{the possessive} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
masculine, direct & \textbf{-\ur{ا}} & \textbf{\ur{ہمارا} \ur{کمرہ}} \\
feminine & \textbf{-\ur{ی}} & \textbf{\ur{ہماری} \ur{ماں}} \\
oblique or plural & \textbf{-\ur{ے}} & \textbf{\ur{ہمارے} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the same three-way agreement chapter thirteen taught for colours, applied to a postposition. Nothing new to learn — one rule paying twice.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hamārā kamrā}
  \item the three faces of one construction — \emph{āp kā}, \emph{merā}, \emph{hamārā}
  \item agreeing with a feminine noun — \emph{hamārī māṅ}
  \item agreeing with an oblique — \emph{hamāre kamre meṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces is \textbf{\ur{ہمارا}} made of? (\textbf{\ur{ہم}} and \textbf{\ur{کا}}, fused.) Which possessive is written as two words? (\textbf{\ur{آپ} \ur{کا}}.) And what does the ending agree with? (\textbf{The noun after it} — gender, and oblique or not.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kamre · kamroṅ · ham · hamārā]{More than one}

\label{lesson:UR-R25-more-than-one}



\begin{quote}
Say all four shapes of \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}}. Two of them are spelled the same — which two, and what tells them apart?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the four cells — \emph{kamrā}, \emph{kamre}, \emph{kamre meṅ}, \emph{kamroṅ meṅ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ham yahāṅ haiṅ}, then \emph{hamārā kamrā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the possessive agreeing three ways — \emph{hamārā kamrā}, \emph{hamārī māṅ}, \emph{hamāre kamre meṅ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the postposition that puts a thing inside another — \emph{meṅ}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — three chapters of endings, run cold}
Three chapters ago no Urdu noun in this book had ever changed shape, been more than one, or been anywhere. Run all of it, cold.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the shape ladder — \emph{kamrā}, \emph{kamre}, \emph{kamroṅ}
  \item the wardrobe, placed — \emph{ṭopī kamre meṅ}, \emph{ṭopī un kamroṅ meṅ}
  \item the pantry — \emph{dūdh yahāṅ hai}, \emph{dūdh vahāṅ nahīṅ hai}
  \item the weather — \emph{bārish hai}, and \emph{yahāṅ bārish hai}
  \item the ear that finally moves — \emph{kān}, then \emph{kānoṅ ko}
  \item colours following the noun over — \emph{kāle kamre meṅ}, \emph{nīle kamroṅ meṅ}
  \item all the possessives — \emph{merā}, \emph{hamārā}, \emph{āp kā}
  \item the demonstratives bending — \emph{is kamre meṅ}, \emph{un kamroṅ meṅ}
  \item I, and we — \emph{maiṅ yahāṅ hūṅ}, \emph{ham yahāṅ haiṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending means \emph{plural, and a postposition is coming}? (\textbf{-\ur{وں}}.) Which two of the four cells collide, and what settles them? (\textbf{Plural direct and oblique singular}; \textbf{whether a postposition follows}.) What is \textbf{\ur{ہمارا}} made of? (\textbf{\ur{ہم}} and \textbf{\ur{کا}}.) And which three words in this book use a plural form for one person? (\textbf{\ur{آپ}}, \textbf{\ur{ان}}, \textbf{\ur{ہم}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
